title: Why must you subscribe to a reactive chain in tests (using `StepVerifier` to assert `expectNext`/`expectError`/`verifyComplete`), and what happens if you never subscribe?
shortTitle: Why you must subscribe to a reactive chain in tests with StepVerifier, and what happens if you never subscribe

s1_definition.profdef: In Project Reactor, a `Mono` or `Flux` is lazy and cold by default: declaring the chain of operators only builds a recipe, and nothing actually runs until a subscriber subscribes. In a test you must trigger that subscription, and `StepVerifier` is the tool designed for it — `StepVerifier.create(publisher)` subscribes to the publisher, then you assert the emitted sequence with `expectNext`, assert failures with `expectError`, and drive the terminal signal with `verifyComplete` or `verify`. The terminal `verify` call is what both subscribes and blocks the test thread until the sequence finishes. If you never subscribe — for example you build the chain and simply let it go out of scope, or you forget the terminal `verify` — the chain never executes, no side effects happen, your assertions are never evaluated, and the test passes vacuously while having tested nothing.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a reactive chain at the National Bank of India like a money-transfer instruction form that Rajesh fills out. Writing the form — debit this account, credit that one, send a receipt — does not move any money. The form just sits there as a set of instructions. Money only moves when someone actually submits the form to the teller, who then processes each step. A `Mono` or `Flux` is exactly that form: declaring it builds the instructions but moves nothing. Subscribing is submitting the form to the teller. In a test, `StepVerifier` is the teller: it submits the form, watches each step happen in order, checks that the right amounts appeared (expectNext), that the right error occurred if you expected one (expectError), and that the transaction closed cleanly (verifyComplete). If you fill out the form and never hand it to the teller, nothing happens — no money moves, no steps run — and if your test forgets to submit it, your test is checking a form that was never processed, so it passes while proving nothing.
s1_definition.oneliner: A reactive chain is a lazy recipe that runs only when subscribed; StepVerifier subscribes and the terminal verify both triggers execution and blocks until done — forget to subscribe and your test passes having tested nothing.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Project Reactor, a `Mono` or `Flux` is lazy and cold by default: declaring the chain of operators only builds a recipe, and nothing actually runs until a subscriber subscribes. In a test you must trigger that subscription, and `StepVerifier` is the tool designed for it — `StepVerifier.create(publisher)` subscribes to the publisher, then you assert the emitted sequence with `expectNext`, assert failures with `expectError`, and drive the terminal signal with `verifyComplete` or `verify`. The terminal `verify` call is what both subscribes and blocks the test thread until the sequence finishes. If you never subscribe — for example you build the chain and simply let it go out of scope, or you forget the terminal `verify` — the chain never executes, no side effects happen, your assertions are never evaluated, and the test passes vacuously while having tested nothing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a reactive chain at the National Bank of India like a money-transfer instruction form that Rajesh fills out. Writing the form — debit this account, credit that one, send a receipt — does not move any money. The form just sits there as a set of instructions. Money only moves when someone actually submits the form to the teller, who then processes each step. A `Mono` or `Flux` is exactly that form: declaring it builds the instructions but moves nothing. Subscribing is submitting the form to the teller. In a test, `StepVerifier` is the teller: it submits the form, watches each step happen in order, checks that the right amounts appeared (expectNext), that the right error occurred if you expected one (expectError), and that the transaction closed cleanly (verifyComplete). If you fill out the form and never hand it to the teller, nothing happens — no money moves, no steps run — and if your test forgets to submit it, your test is checking a form that was never processed, so it passes while proving nothing.

**One line to remember:** A reactive chain is a lazy recipe that runs only when subscribed; StepVerifier subscribes and the terminal verify both triggers execution and blocks until done — forget to subscribe and your test passes having tested nothing.

sections.s2_technical:
The foundation is that Reactor publishers are lazy. When you write `accountRepo.findById(id).map(Account::getBalance).filter(b -> b.signum() > 0)`, you have not executed anything. You have assembled an operator chain — a blueprint describing what should happen when data flows. No repository call is made, no mapping runs, no side effect fires. This laziness is deliberate: it lets Reactor compose, schedule, and optimize the whole pipeline, and it is why the same publisher can be subscribed multiple times. The practical consequence is that the terminal operation — subscription — is mandatory to make anything happen.

Subscription is the act that pushes a `Subscriber` into the chain and requests data, which causes the source to start emitting. In production your subscription often happens implicitly: when you return a `Mono` from a Spring WebFlux controller, the framework subscribes for you, and when you return it from an R2DBC flow the adapter subscribes. But in a unit test there is no framework subscribing on your behalf, so if you just call the method that returns the `Mono` and do nothing with it, the chain is never subscribed and never runs. This is the number-one reactive testing bug: a test that looks like it exercises logic but actually executes none of it.

`StepVerifier` exists precisely to subscribe and assert in a controlled way. `StepVerifier.create(publisher)` wraps the publisher and prepares a subscriber. You then declare expectations step by step: `expectNext(value)` asserts the next emitted item equals the value, `expectNextMatches(predicate)` asserts it satisfies a condition, `expectError(SomeException.class)` asserts the sequence terminates with that error, and `expectComplete`/`verifyComplete` asserts it finished without error. The crucial detail is the terminal method. `verify()`, `verifyComplete()`, and `verifyError()` are the methods that actually trigger the subscription and block the calling thread until the sequence reaches a terminal signal or a timeout. If you build a `StepVerifier` with expectations but forget to call a terminal `verify`, nothing subscribes, nothing runs, and the assertions are never checked — the test passes vacuously. This is a subtle trap because the code compiles and looks complete.

What happens concretely if you never subscribe: the publisher's work never starts, so any side effect inside the chain — a database write, a counter increment, a log line — never happens; any exception the chain would throw is never thrown, so an `assertThrows` wrapped around merely building the chain will fail to see the error; and time-based operators never advance. `StepVerifier` also solves the time problem with `withVirtualTime`, which lets you advance a virtual clock so a chain containing a `delay` or `timeout` can be tested instantly without real waiting, and you still must call the terminal `verify`. The senior nuances: always assert the terminal signal, not just intermediate items, because a chain that emits the right values but then errors is still broken; use `verify(Duration)` to bound tests so a hung chain fails fast rather than blocking the suite; remember that `block()` is an alternative way to subscribe in a test but it only gives you the value or exception, not the fine-grained sequence assertions StepVerifier provides; and be careful with hot publishers and shared mutable state, where multiple subscriptions can change behavior. The single most important habit is to treat the terminal `verify` as non-optional — it is what makes the test real.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, Rajesh writes a reactive transfer service. Money transfers are modeled as reactive chains, and the team keeps writing tests that pass but catch no bugs, so we model exactly why subscription matters.

Problem 1 — A test called the transfer method, which returns a `Mono`, and then asserted on the account balances directly, expecting the debit to have happened. The test passed even when the transfer logic was broken, because the `Mono` was never subscribed, so the debit never ran and the balances were simply unchanged from the start. This is exactly what subscription explains: without it, the side effect inside the chain never fires.

Problem 2 — Another test built a `StepVerifier` with `expectNext` and `expectError` but forgot the terminal `verify()`. It passed no matter what, because without the terminal call nothing subscribed. This is the vacuous-pass trap.

Problem 3 — A test for a transfer that must fail with insufficient funds wrapped `assertThrows` around building the chain, and the error never surfaced because the chain was never executed. This is exactly why you assert errors through `expectError` on a subscribed chain, not by building the chain alone.

The mini-project builds a reactive `TransferService` whose `transfer` returns a `Mono<TransferReceipt>` and performs a debit and credit as side effects, and a chain that errors on insufficient funds. Then we write tests both the wrong way (never subscribing, to show the vacuous pass) and the right way (StepVerifier with a terminal verify) so the difference is concrete and runnable. Characters are Rajesh (SAV2001, 1000000) and Priya (CUR3001, 250000) with a rent transfer.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Run the reactive transfer tests
mvn test -Dtest=TransferServiceTest

# Run everything
mvn clean test

# Key dependencies (pom.xml):
#   io.projectreactor:reactor-core
#   io.projectreactor:reactor-test       (StepVerifier, StepVerifier.withVirtualTime)
#   org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter

# Run the demo that shows "no subscribe = no side effect"
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/reactive-transfer-service-1.0.0.jar
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001) has 1,000,000 and Priya (CUR3001) has 250,000; a rent transfer of 50,000.

Step 1 (wrong way): The test calls `transfer("SAV2001","CUR3001",50000)`, which returns a `Mono`. The chain is assembled — find both accounts, check funds, debit, credit — but nothing subscribes. No code inside the chain runs.

Step 2: The test then reads Rajesh's balance and finds it is still 1,000,000. The assertion "balance equals 1,000,000" passes, but only because the debit never happened. The test looks green while having exercised none of the transfer logic — the vacuous pass.

Step 3 (right way): The test wraps the same `transfer` call in `StepVerifier.create(...)`, declares `expectNextMatches` for a COMPLETED receipt, and calls `verifyComplete()`. That terminal call subscribes, which finally runs the chain: both accounts are found, funds are sufficient, Rajesh is debited to 950,000 and Priya credited to 300,000, and the receipt is emitted.

Step 4: `StepVerifier` checks that the emitted receipt matches and that the sequence completed with no error. Then the follow-up assertions confirm the balances actually changed — 950,000 and 300,000 — proving the side effects ran.

Step 5 (error path): The test requests a 5,000,000 transfer. Through `StepVerifier` with `expectError(InsufficientFundsException.class)` and `verify()`, the chain is subscribed, the funds check fails, the chain emits the error, and `StepVerifier` asserts it. Without the terminal `verify`, the error would never surface.

Step 6: The trap test shows that a `StepVerifier` without a terminal `verify` never subscribes, so it is as good as not testing — the fix is always to end with a terminal `verify`.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-25 03:40:00 INFO    Transferred 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001
TransferServiceTest
 wrongWay_neverSubscribed_vacuousPass   (balance UNCHANGED — chain never ran)
 rightWay_subscribedWithStepVerifier    (950000 / 300000 — side effects ran)
 rightWay_insufficientFundsEmitsError   (InsufficientFundsException surfaced)
 trap_missingTerminalVerify_doesNotRun  (terminal verify() is mandatory)
BUILD SUCCESS — 4 tests, 0 failures
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  ── WITHOUT subscription (vacuous pass) ────────────────────
  service.transfer("SAV2001","CUR3001",50000)
    │ builds operator chain: findById → zipWith → flatMap(debit/credit)
    ▼
  Mono<TransferReceipt>  ── NOBODY SUBSCRIBES ──→  (nothing runs)
    │
    ▼
  balance SAV2001 = 1,000,000 (UNCHANGED)  → assertion passes, bug hidden

  ── WITH StepVerifier (real test) ──────────────────────────
  StepVerifier.create( service.transfer(...) )
    │ .expectNextMatches(status==COMPLETED)
    │ .verifyComplete()   ← TERMINAL: subscribes + blocks
    ▼ subscription pushes demand into the chain
  findById(SAV2001) → Rajesh 1,000,000
  findById(CUR3001) → Priya 250,000
    │ funds ok?
    ├─ YES → debit 50,000 → 950,000 ; credit 50,000 → 300,000 → emit receipt
    └─ NO  → Mono.error(InsufficientFundsException) → expectError asserts it
    ▼
  verifyComplete()/verify() returns → balances truly changed → assertions real
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Reactive Chain Execution & Testing (banking) ═══

   PRODUCTION (framework subscribes for you)
   ┌──────────────┐  Mono   ┌──────────────┐  subscribe  ┌──────────┐
   │ WebFlux       │────────▶│ TransferSvc  │────────────▶│ R2DBC /  │
   │ Controller    │ returns │ (lazy chain) │ (framework) │ repo     │
   └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘             └──────────┘
        ▲ Spring subscribes to the returned Mono → chain runs

   TEST (YOU must subscribe — no framework)
   ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐  subscribe  ┌──────────┐
   │ StepVerifier │────────▶│ TransferSvc  │────────────▶│ in-mem   │
   │ .create(...) │ wraps   │ (lazy chain) │ (verify())  │ repo     │
   │ .expectNext  │         └──────────────┘             └──────────┘
   │ .verify()  ◀── terminal call = subscribe + block
   └──────────────┘
      If you skip subscription → chain never runs → test passes vacuously.

  Rule: lazy publisher needs a subscriber; in tests StepVerifier's terminal
  verify is that subscriber. Always assert the terminal signal.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — StepVerifier Usage (banking) ═══

  ┌─ Principles ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Laziness: Mono/Flux = recipe, runs only on subscribe     │
  │  Terminal-signal assertion: check complete/error, not     │
  │     just emitted items                                    │
  │  Bounded verify: verify(Duration) so hung chains fail fast│
  │  Virtual time: withVirtualTime for delay/timeout operators│
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── StepVerifier API (with usage) ──────────────────────────

  StepVerifier.create(publisher)          subscribes to the chain
    .expectNext(v)                         next item equals v
    .expectNextMatches(pred)               next item satisfies predicate
    .expectError(Ex.class)                 terminates with that error
    .expectComplete()                      completes with no error
    .verify()         ← TERMINAL: triggers subscription + blocks
    .verifyComplete() ← TERMINAL shortcut for expectComplete + verify
    .verifyError(Ex.class) ← TERMINAL shortcut for expectError + verify

  ── State Diagram: a Mono under test ───────────────────────

  [ASSEMBLED] ──no subscribe──→ [NEVER_RUNS] → vacuous pass (BUG)
       │ StepVerifier terminal verify()
       ▼
  [SUBSCRIBED] ──data path──→ [NEXT emitted] → [COMPLETED]
       │                                   assert expectNext + verifyComplete
       └──error path──→ [ERROR emitted] → assert expectError + verify

  ── Call Chain (right way) ─────────────────────────────────

  1. StepVerifier.create(service.transfer("SAV2001","CUR3001",50000))
  2.   .expectNextMatches(r -> r.status==COMPLETED)
  3.   .verifyComplete()        → SUBSCRIBE happens here
  4.     → findById x2 → funds ok → debit 950000 / credit 300000 → emit
  5.     → StepVerifier asserts emission + completion
  6. follow-up assertEquals balances → 950000 / 300000 (side effects real)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
In Project Reactor a Mono or Flux is lazy and cold by default, which means declaring the chain of operators only builds a recipe and nothing actually runs until something subscribes. When I write a chain like find the account, map to the balance, then debit it, I have not executed a single step — I have only described what should happen when data flows. Subscription is the act that pushes a subscriber into the chain and requests data, which is what finally makes the source emit and the operators run. In production the framework usually subscribes for me, for example when I return a Mono from a WebFlux controller Spring subscribes to it. But in a unit test there is no framework subscribing on my behalf, so I have to trigger it myself.

StepVerifier is the tool built for exactly that. StepVerifier.create wraps the publisher and prepares a subscriber, then I declare expectations step by step — expectNext to assert the next emitted item, expectNextMatches to assert it satisfies a condition, expectError to assert the sequence fails with a specific exception, and verifyComplete to assert it finished cleanly. The single most important detail is the terminal method. verify, verifyComplete, and verifyError are the calls that actually trigger the subscription and block the test thread until the sequence reaches a terminal signal. If I build a StepVerifier with all the right expectations but forget the terminal verify, nothing subscribes, nothing runs, and the assertions are never checked, so the test passes while having tested absolutely nothing.

If I never subscribe at all, the consequences are concrete. Any side effect inside the chain, like a database write or a balance change, never happens. Any exception the chain would throw is never thrown, so wrapping assertThrows around merely building the chain will never see the error. And time-based operators never advance. That is why the correct habit is to always route the chain through a subscribed StepVerifier and always assert the terminal signal, not just the intermediate items, because a chain that emits the right values and then errors is still broken. I also bound my tests with verify of a duration so a hung chain fails fast, and I use withVirtualTime when the chain has delays or timeouts so I can advance a virtual clock instead of waiting in real time.

At the National Bank of India this bit us on the reactive transfer service, and it is the clearest example I give. A teammate wrote a test that called the transfer method, which returns a Mono, and then asserted on the account balances expecting the debit to have happened. The test passed even when the transfer logic was completely broken, because the Mono was never subscribed, so the debit never ran and the balance was simply unchanged from the start — a dangerous false green. We fixed it by routing the call through StepVerifier.create with expectNextMatches for a completed receipt and a verifyComplete terminal call, which actually subscribed and ran the chain, so Rajesh was really debited from one million to nine hundred fifty thousand and Priya credited to three hundred thousand, and only then did the balance assertions mean anything. For the insufficient-funds case we used expectError with a terminal verify so the exception actually surfaced. The rule I now enforce in reviews is simple: a reactive test without a terminal verify is not a test, because the chain never ran.
